vignette:
Bao presents as a gentle and soft-spoken 72-year-old man, a demeanor that serves him well in his work as a nanny for a young family. He speaks of the two children in his care with a quiet affection that is immediately apparent. This gentleness, however, is a carefully constructed fortress against a state of inner turmoil that has governed his life for over forty years. Before he met his wife, Lien, and built the stable life he now has, Bao was in a relationship with a man who was volatile and violent. The trauma stems from a period of several months where the physical abuse was a near-daily occurrence, often happening at night when his partner would return home angry and unpredictable. Bao recalls one night in particular, being woken from sleep and pinned to the bed, unable to see his partner's face in the pitch-black room, only feeling the weight of him and the sharp impacts of his fists.

In the years that followed, the memories of that time began to intrude. He describes them not as his own, but as watching a film of something terrible that happened to a different, weaker man. Yet, when these images surface, the terror is entirely his. A flashback brings with it the same gut-wrenching fear he felt in that dark room, his heart pounding as if he is once again trapped and helpless. This profound sense of threat has never fully subsided; Bao lives in a state of constant, exhausting hypervigilance. He is unable to relax, even sitting in his own armchair with Lien beside him. He feels perpetually jumpy, and any unexpected movement in his vicinity-a bird flying past the window, one of the children dashing past him-causes him to flinch with a surge of panic, his body reacting as if an attack is imminent.

The sheer horror of the memories and the persistent feeling of being unsafe have led Bao to develop a rigid set of rules for living. To prevent the terror of recall, he began to meticulously avoid any circumstance that reminded him of the trauma. He cannot be in dark rooms; at his job, he leaves the nap-time routine to the children's mother, unable to step into their dimly lit bedrooms. This constant state of being on guard is so draining that he also avoids anything he perceives as potentially stressful, which has shrunk his world considerably. Most significantly, he came to believe that anger itself was the danger. He equates the rage he saw in his former partner with the emotion itself, and so he has spent decades systematically suppressing any flicker of it in himself, convinced that to feel anger is to become dangerous.

These strategies have become a self-reinforcing trap. Living in a state of high alert means his mind is always primed for danger. A child's sudden movement triggers the jolt of fear, and in that moment of panic, the memories have a clear path in. When a flashback does break through, his body reenacts the trauma; he feels his shoulders hunch and his arms instinctively come up to shield his head, the same defensive posture he was forced into all those years ago. This physical reenactment makes the memory feel terrifyingly present, which in turn drives him deeper into his avoidance. His refusal to enter a dark room is a constant, physical reminder of why he has the rule, which itself can trigger the very memories he is trying to keep at bay.

The life he has built is beginning to fray under the strain. Lien worries about his increasing isolation, and an incident at work has left him deeply shaken. A few weeks ago, the five-year-old boy he cares for jumped out from behind a sofa to surprise him. Bao's reaction was not one of playful shock, but of pure terror; he cried out and stumbled backward, his face pale with fear. The sight of the child's startled, worried face filled him with a profound shame. It was this moment, the realization that his past was now actively harming the present he holds so dear, that finally propelled him to seek help. He is terrified of losing his job, but more than that, he is terrified of living the rest of his life as a prisoner in his own body.
